newsitem.title: SOUTH KOREA: S.Korean government urges unions not to strike.
newsitem.headline: S.Korean government urges unions not to strike.

text.p: The South Korean government on Thursday issued a last minute appeal to militant unions to call off planned strikes that could paralyse large sections of the country's export industries.
Meanwhile, the country's largest employer's group urged members to replace striking workers, setting up a potentially explosive confrontation.

The outlawed Korea Confederation of Trade Unions has threatened a four-hour stoppage on Friday to be followed by an indefinite walkout on Monday in protest to revisions of labour law allowing layoffs and flexible work hours.
Its larger counterpart, the more conservative Korea Federation of Trade Unions, said it would call out its union affiliates for one hour on Monday and three hours on Thursday.
"Although we are sympathetic to labour, given the current difficulty of the economy, we ask they refrain from industrial action," a ruling New Korea Party statement said.
"It's impossible to satisfy both management and labour. So we appeal to both sides...to share the pain."
Both umbrella union bodies object to the first revisions in the labour law for 43 years that they say threaten jobs.
The outlawed union body claims 500,000 members at about 300 companies, including Hyundai Motor Co, Kia Motors Corp, Hyundai Heavy Industries Co, and Daewoo Heavy Industries Co.
The federation claims 1.2 million members at 800 firms, including LG Electronics, Daewoo Electronics, Oriental Brewery and Hankook Tire.
"It's not clear whether the unions will actually strike tomorrow, but if they do, we will have to respond in some way," said an official at the Korea Employers' Federation.

In a toughly-worded statement, the employer's federation called on companies to "bring strict punishment, according to company guidelines, to those employees participating in any strikes, report them to authorities, or press legal action for compensation if necessary."
Members were also urged to bring in replacement workers or shut down lines if necessary.
South Korea's three main opposition parties called for a delay in pushing through a new labour bill containing a number of controversial revisions.
The New Korea Party wants the bill passed during the current National Assembly session, which ends on December 18.
But a joint statement by the National Congress for New Politics, United Liberal Democrats and the Democratic Party said the timetable was too short.

"The government submitted the revised labour law on Tuesday, only seven days before the end of the session. It is impossible to seriously consider the law given the technical aspects of the revision and the shortage of time," the statement said.
It suggested an extraordinary parliamentary session be held in February to decide the matter.

Park In-sang, chairman of the larger union body, on Wednesday began an indefinite hunger strike. On Thursday, the group handed a petition signed by 722,617 workers to the office of the National Assembly Speaker.
Management is unhappy with labour revisions that would allow multiple trade unions in each workplace, saying it would lead to increased militancy as unions vied for members.
Industrial action would be a major blow to an economy suffering from an export slowdown led by plunging international prices for memory chips, steel and petrochemical products.
"The impact could be quite substantial. It of course depends entirely on the duration and the scope of the strikes," said Steve Marvin, head of research at Ssangyong Securities.
